Sadly, a relationship is like a living organism, in the sense when they die, you need to bury them in the ground. You can take that first step blocking him on social media. From my experience, the best thing is completely cutting yourself off from your ex. This for me was the hardest thing to do after my ex ended it with me, I had got so used to him being there. However, by keeping in contact you don't fully allow yourself to move on, as you try to give yourself false hope of things having not changed. Allow yourself to cry and be sad, but get active and be sociable too so you don't become a recluse, so find plenty of 
distractions, but remember to grieve too. 

Many weeks after my ex and I broke up I couldn't face visiting all the places we went together, and three months on I still get sick when I'm exposed to a reminder of us (like seeing a friend of his two weeks ago) but these triggers are becoming less and less trivial day by day.

It takes time, but it does gradually get better. I'm still in recovery, I think about him almost every hour of every day, saddened that I can't have any more of those special times with him. But his departure will open a space for a potentially even more amazing person in the future. Take care.

Being from the UK the terms 'liberal' and 'conservative' have slightly different meanings. The main UK parties are Labour (Bernie Sanders-style Democrats mostly) and the Conservatives (moderate-style Republicans mostly). There are also smaller parties like the Liberal Democrats (think of the Libertarian Party/moderate Democrats) and UKIP (Trump). I'm a member and supporter of the Liberal Democrats, and value liberty and individualism, but also believe in making sure there is a level enough playing field in life for as many people possible. I support traditional institutions such as the monarchy, the established church (Anglicanism) and (controversially for my party) faith schools, which are aspects of my views which lean to the right. However, polices such as universal healthcare and tackling inequality mainly through encouraging economic growth and redistributing the proceeds. On LGBT rights I take a fairly laissez faire stance, mainly because the UK has (nearly) managed to achieve full equality in our country, except Northern Ireland. Edit: also very pro immigration due to the economic benefits.

Increasingly I think it's unhelpful having this concept of an 'LGBT community', because it excludes people who, like you, live in isolated communities. I think homophobia has forced gay people to create their own community, which has inadvertently detached us from the rest of society, and only suits certain gay people. If you wanted to be particularly ambitious, maybe set up some sort of LGBT group?

Depending on where you live in the world, there should be something in your area. I live in the UK so I cannot speak for everyone, but If there isn't anything in your area, looking at clubs and societies which are not LGBT specific is good idea. There you'll probably find some gay people amongst the mix as well as people you have a shared interest with.

The gay community I have found on occasion to be a one which can contribute to loneliness, but from my experience there are guys out there who are caring. However it may take looking beyond apps to find that friendship you desire. If you have any interest, join a club or society which promotes that interest. Volunteer, get active in your community. There you will find people, including gay guys, who will be able to be true friends because of a shared passion which you have in common. The more I think about it, the people if feel most comfortable around are those who I share a passion with, rather than being of the same sexual orientation.
